blurb: The physical side of AI: power-hungry racks, cooling, electricity demand and the gigawatt build-out.

cards.title: A factory for computation

steps.p: A traditional server rack drew perhaps 5–15 kW. A rack of NVIDIA's GB200 NVL72 systems draws around 120 kW.
Nearly every watt consumed becomes heat that must be removed. Power delivery and cooling dominate the building's design.
Thousands of optical links tie GPUs together so they can act like one giant computer.

cards.aside: AI data centers are increasingly described by their power capacity — megawatts and gigawatts — rather than by floor space.

cards.q: Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) is total facility power divided by IT equipment power. A PUE of 1.1 means…
options: About 10% extra power goes to cooling and other overhead
cards.why: 10% overhead. A perfect facility would score 1.0. Modern hyperscale sites run around 1.1–1.2; older enterprise data centers are often far higher.

cards.statement: Liquid cooling is becoming standard for the newest, densest AI racks.
cards.why: True. Air cannot carry away 100+ kW from a single rack efficiently. Direct-to-chip liquid cooling pipes coolant through plates on the GPUs.

cards.title: xAI said it built its "Colossus" supercomputer in Memphis with 100,000 GPUs in 122 days.
cards.detail: Such projects usually take years. To get power quickly, the site initially relied partly on on-site gas turbines, which drew local environmental objections.

cards.statement: Where AI data centers get built is driven mainly by cheap land.
cards.why: False. The binding constraint is access to large amounts of electricity — and how quickly the grid can connect a new site. Land is a minor cost.

cards.q: Roughly how much more power does a modern AI rack draw than a typical traditional server rack?
cards.why: Around 10× or more. Roughly 120 kW versus 5–15 kW. That jump forces new electrical and cooling designs, not just more of the same.

cards.title: How much power AI uses

steps.p: The International Energy Agency estimated data centers used about 415 TWh in 2024 — around 1.5% of global electricity.
Its 2025 projection: roughly doubling to about 945 TWh by 2030, with AI the main driver.
Demand clusters in certain regions, like northern Virginia and Ireland, where data centers take a large share of local power.

cards.aside: Globally modest, locally enormous: that is the shape of the AI energy story.

cards.q: According to the IEA, what share of global electricity did data centers use in 2024?
cards.why: About 1.5%. Significant and growing fast, but still smaller than sectors like industry or buildings. The concern is the growth rate and local concentration.

cards.statement: A typical chatbot query uses about as much energy as boiling a kettle.
cards.why: False. Recent estimates for a typical text query are around 0.3 watt-hours. Boiling a kettle takes roughly 100 Wh — hundreds of times more. Long reasoning or video generation costs much more.

cards.q: For a widely used model, which typically uses more energy over its lifetime?
cards.why: Serving. Training is a huge one-time cost, but answering billions of queries for months or years usually adds up to more.

cards.title: Microsoft agreed to buy power from a restarted reactor at Three Mile Island to supply its data centers.
cards.detail: The 2024 deal covers Unit 1 — not the reactor damaged in the 1979 accident — which had shut down in 2019 for economic reasons. It was renamed the Crane Clean Energy Center.

cards.statement: Major tech companies have signed agreements to buy power from small modular nuclear reactors.
cards.why: True. Google agreed with Kairos Power and Amazon invested in X-energy in 2024, betting on reactors that are not yet operating commercially.

cards.title: Where the heat goes

steps.p: Many data centers cool by evaporating water, which absorbs a lot of heat but consumes water permanently.
Liquid-cooled systems circulate the same coolant and reject heat through dry coolers, using little water but more electricity.
Power plants that supply the electricity also use water, so a site's footprint is larger than its own meter shows.

cards.aside: Building water-cooled sites in dry regions has become a local political issue.

cards.q: Why do evaporative cooling systems consume water rather than just circulate it?
options: Heat is removed by evaporating water, which leaves as vapor
cards.why: Evaporation carries heat away. Turning water to vapor absorbs a lot of energy, which is why it is so effective — and why the water is gone afterwards.

cards.statement: All of a data center's water footprint comes from its on-site cooling.
cards.why: False. Generating its electricity also uses water, often a large share. Full accounting includes both direct and indirect use.

cards.q: Liquid cooling works so much better than air mainly because water…
options: Carries thousands of times more heat per unit volume
cards.why: Heat capacity. By volume, water absorbs about 3,500 times more heat than air for the same temperature rise, so small pipes replace huge airflows.

cards.title: Microsoft once ran a sealed data center on the seabed off Scotland's Orkney Islands.
cards.detail: Project Natick's two-year experiment ending in 2020 found servers failed at one-eighth the rate of a land-based control group, possibly thanks to the stable temperature and a nitrogen atmosphere.

cards.q: Some Nordic data centers reduce waste by…
options: Piping their waste heat into district heating networks for homes
cards.why: Heat reuse. Server heat warms nearby buildings through district heating, turning a waste stream into a resource.

cards.title: Building at unprecedented scale

steps.p: Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta together spent over $200 billion on capital expenditure in 2024, largely for AI infrastructure.
In January 2025, OpenAI, SoftBank and Oracle announced Stargate, pledging up to $500 billion over four years for US AI infrastructure.
Single sites are now planned in gigawatts — the output of a large power station.

cards.aside: The bottlenecks have shifted from chips to power, transformers and grid connections.

cards.statement: One gigawatt of data center capacity draws roughly the output of a large nuclear reactor.
cards.why: True. A typical large reactor produces about 1 GW. Several planned AI campuses aim for one or more gigawatts each.

cards.q: Why do grid interconnection queues matter so much for AI data centers?
options: Connecting a large new load can take years, delaying projects even when chips are ready
cards.why: Time to power. New transmission lines and substations take years, so developers chase sites with spare capacity or build their own generation.

cards.q: Stargate, announced in January 2025, pledged up to how much investment?
cards.why: Up to $500 billion over four years, starting with a campus in Abilene, Texas. Its full scale depends on financing that was still being arranged.

cards.title: Hyperscalers' capital spending on AI rivals the largest infrastructure programs in history.
cards.detail: Annual spending of hundreds of billions of dollars exceeds what most countries spend on all their roads and railways, raising questions about whether demand will justify it.

cards.title: Estimate a cluster's power
cards.body: An H100 draws up to 700 W. Running all year that is about 6 MWh. Multiply by GPU count, then add 20–50% for servers, networking and cooling.
cards.challenge: Estimate the power for 100,000 GPUs at 700 W each before overhead. (Answer: 70 MW — the scale of a small city.)
